conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You came in with high fevers and right thigh pain—can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was home and started feeling really sick—fever, chills, nausea. My thigh pain came back, right where the old hematoma was.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were just discharged two weeks ago after that hematoma and the SVC procedure. Any facial swelling this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not this time. Just the fever and the pain. It scared me—I didn’t know if it was serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’re going to check things out. We’ve already done blood work and a chest X-ray. The X-ray looks clear—no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. But why the fever? I was fine at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know yet. Could be infection, inflammation, or even a flare of your Crohn’s. We’ll keep monitoring and run more tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the thigh pain? Is the hematoma back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We ordered an ultrasound. It should help us see if there’s a new hematoma or something else going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound is back. Good news—the old hematoma is completely gone. No sign of it in the groin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then why does my thigh still hurt so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we’re trying to figure out. The pain could be from muscle strain, nerve irritation, or a small new bleed. We’ll keep watching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been vomiting too—green stuff. That’s not normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bilious vomiting. That’s concerning. Could mean your stomach isn’t emptying well. We might need a CT scan to check your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did the CT scan. Your colon looks okay—no Crohn’s flare or blockage. But there’s a small fluid collection in your right thigh.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it another hematoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. It’s small—about 3 cm. Not like the big one before. We’ll watch it, but it doesn’t need surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vomiting? Is it from my Crohn’s?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of obstruction or Crohn’s flare on the scan. More likely gastric dysmotility—your stomach isn’t moving food well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you here for a few days. We’ve placed an NG tube to help your stomach rest and reduce vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The NG tube is working. You’re not vomiting as much. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but the Dilaudid helps. I’m just tired of being in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re watching you closely. Your fever hasn’t returned, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs are stable. White count was a bit high yesterday but is improving. No infection found in blood cultures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the fever was just a one-time thing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looks that way. Sometimes fevers happen without a clear cause, especially with complex medical histories like yours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Crohn’s? Is it acting up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. The CT showed no inflammation, strictures, or fistulas. Your Crohn’s seems quiet right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to try removing the NG tube today. Your stomach seems to be moving better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. I hate this tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips. If you keep them down, we’ll slowly increase. But if you vomit, we might need it back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well overnight—no vomiting. We’ll advance your diet to soft foods today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. How’s my thigh?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The small fluid area is stable. It’s likely resolving on its own. Pain should improve with time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds? I’m on so many.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping your thyroid, vitamin, and Crohn’s meds. We’ll adjust the Dilaudid and Benadryl with a taper plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Taper? Why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To avoid withdrawal. You’ve been on them for pain and nausea. We’ll slowly reduce the dose so your body adjusts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news. You’ve kept down solid food, no vomiting. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s wonderful. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the Dilaudid taper as written—start every 4 hours as needed, then slowly space it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Benadryl shot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get injections at first, then taper to oral. We’ll send supplies home with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my port? Do I still need to flush it with alcohol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, daily with 10% ethanol to prevent infections, especially with your history. Then flush with saline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’ll discharge you in a few hours. Keep up with your PCP appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was so anxious coming in, but you’ve been great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here for you. Call if you have chest pain, bloody vomit, or trouble breathing. Otherwise, rest and follow the taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your warfarin dose stays the same. Keep monitoring INR with your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And take calcium with vitamin D as before. Your levels were low, so it’s important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over discharge papers and meds. You’re cleared to leave by 1 PM.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one more thing—should I worry about the fever coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s unlikely. If it does, or if pain worsens, call your doctor. But right now, you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll watch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep using the oxazepam if anxiety flares. Hospital stays can be tough with your PTSD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been hard. But I feel safer going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ve noted that in your record so future teams are aware.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You’re strong—you’ve been through a lot. Now focus on healing at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.
